subtopic: QUESTION OF ADMISSION OR READMISSION TO RELIEF CAMPS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). In a Vancouver paper which arrived this morning I notice a news item indicating that a number of men who have left unemployment relief camps to seek work in Vancouver are stranded in that city and are refused readmission to the camps. I understand that the relief camp bureau which takes applications from homeless single men in Vancouver has been closed, and that the men now coming into the city cannot make application to go into the camps.
The provincial and municipal governments, as previously, have refused to accept any responsibility for these men. Would the minister outline the government's policy in the matter?
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was kind enough to advise me of his intention to ask this question, and I have also read the newspaper item to which he has referred.
In carrying out the policy which was outlined to this house on February 26, no more men are being admitted to the relief camps either in British Columbia or any other part of Canada, the intention of the government being to close the camps at as early a date as possible. To admit or readmit men to the camps would defeat the object of the arrangements already made.
In the meantime, until the camps are closed, the personnel, formerly receiving 20 cents a day, are receiving in addition to their food, clothing, tobacco, medical attention and other perquisites, an allowance of $15 monthly.
It appears that a small number of men having left the camps of their own accord, prior to the announcement of (he new policy, are now represented as being stranded in the city of Vancouver. This matter had already been brought to the attention of the government by the premier of British Columbia, and Minister of Labour for the province, as well as by the mayor of Vancouver, and perhaps I may read the reply sent to his worship on March 14, which was as follows:
Labour department most unwilling to create precedent by departure from policy of no admissions to camps. Cannot make too plain that black list has nothing to do with policy as no applicants of any kind are being admitted anywhere in Canada. Statistics indicate that local relief problem already lightened to extent 500 or 600 men by dominion policy as records indicate that fewer men to that number have left camps this spring in search of jobs in competition with local relief cases. Men refuse to leave camps because of new policy of refusing readmission. Under circumstances consider it advisable that city and province care for these 60 odd men temporarily pending further negotiations if necessary.
I may say that in the communications received from the city of Vancouver it was represented that the number of men stranded was in the vicinity of 65, and in the newspaper report it was represented I believe as being nearly 175.
Prior to December 1, the province received a grant in aid from the federal treasury of $150,000 monthly, which was increased as from December 1 to $262,500, during the months of December, January, Februaiy and

March, for the purpose of assisting the province in discharging its responsibilities for the relief of necessitous persons within its borders, it being provided by the order in council authorizing the grant that the province should assist the municipalities financially to such extent as may be necessary, this increase having been made following the representations made at the dominion-provincial conference of December 9th-13th.

They have stated that we need a protective tariff for these goods because we have not a home market, and the people who did have a good home market could ship into this country.

You never heard me
say that.

Then the hon.
member differs with his colleagues. The fact that we have a good home market for agricultural implements surely does not mean that we should put a high tariff against them and charge our people more for their implements.
Then the hon. member said that if one of the agricultural implement plants happened to be in Moose Jaw possibly I would see eye to eye with them. All I have to say is that there are industries in Moose Jaw, as well as in other parts of western Canada, and as the hon. member for that city and constituency

may I say that if any of those industries are being protected to a point detrimental to the Canadian people as a whole, I would ask the government here and now to take off the protection.

May I say a word to the
lion, member for Davenport. I have no doubt that he is sincere in his effort to help the working people of Canada, and that he believes that by the imposition of high tariffs Canadians will be provided with steady employment. Of course the reverse argument would be that in countries where there are no tariffs there would be no employment. Such is not the case. I would point out that there is very little relationship between high tariffs and employment. If high tariffs provided employment then surely between 1930 and 1935 there would have been no unemployment in Canada. In those years we increased our tariffs to almost unknown heights.
In the hon. member's observations he seemed to have three ideas to place before the committee. The first was that in the United States there is almost unanimous opinion in favour of the agreement. I do not think he is quite correct in assuming that the little pamphlet from Chicago which he has in his possession represents the opinion of the whole of the United States. From reading journals and papers of the United States I know there has been a strong volume of opinion in opposition to the agreement. In the month of January, when the terms of the agreement were made public, they went so far as to threaten legal proceedings to upset it, their allegation being that the President of the United States was not properly exercising the powers conferred upon him. Evidently the statement the hon. member is attempting to convey, namely, that people in the United States are unanimously in favour of the agreement, is not quite in accordance with the facts.
Then the hon. member spoke about the stabilization of the tariff. I have never known him to be in favour of a stabilized tariff, and this is the first occasion I have heard him advocate this in the House of Commons. To my knowledge he has always voted against stabilization. Between 1930 and 1935 he voted in favour of increases, a procedure which did not have the effect of stabilization. Apparently his idea, of a stable tariff is one whereby it will remain at its present high level. In his view, so long as we keep on increasing it there will be no difficulty, but if we attempt to decrease it we ought to take steps to bring about a stable tariff.
His third .point had to do with benefits created by certain industries establishing

themselves in some of our western cities. He said that if one of the implement companies would establish itself in Saskatoon or Moose Jaw-*
Regina and Saskatoon.

I will come to Regina, later. He said that if one of these industries would establish itself in a western city it would confer upon that city almost untold benefits, and that some of the harsh feelings held by western people concerning eastern manufacturers might be softened. May I tell the hon. member that western cities are full of these factories, and some of them are not the boons or blessings he supposes. May I point out an incident of the last few years. The city of Regina was very anxious to have a General Motors' factory locate at that point, and offered attractive concessions. I believe the city gave some relief from taxation and, if I am not mistaken, provided the company with a cheap site. Probably hon. members from Saskatchewan could give more details than I could. I do know however that instead of being a blessing the factory in Regina is probably the very reverse. While they are operating three or four months of the year and during that time provide employment, it costs the city far more in relief expenditures to keep the employees during those long periods when they are not engaged in the plant. What happened in Regina has happened at different points in western Canada. One might gather from the observations of the hon. member for Davenport that the manufacturer in Canada is a kind of philanthropist, and that he operates his factory simply to give employment to workmen.
Nonsense.

I think one might draw
that inference from the hon. member's observation. I say that they aTe nothing of the kind. The manufacturer will open a factory or a workshop wherever he sees an opportunity of selling his wares. The labourer is only a secondary consideration. The opportunity of selling wares was the motivating power behind the opening of the plants in Regina and other parts of western Canada. The chief point we have to remember is that no amount of tariff can provide jobs in Canada for the working people. I am speaking in the aggregate, and admit that here and there one may find an isolated case in which high tariff protection may create a factory and give employment. In the long run, however, it may do more harm than good. It may be true that while in some

cases we might send money to the United States, it comes back in other directions. I suggest that it comes back by means of the tourist traffic. This traffic has become one of the greatest industries of Canada, and in one of the last years for which we have the figures we derived approximately $200,000,000 therefrom. In more prosperous years we received approximately $300,000,000.
When we are discussing this matter I believe we should have in our minds a clear perspective of t>he meaning of tariff protection. I suggest that so far as labour is concerned it means very little, but that it means a great deal to the owners of industry. As the hon. member for Davenport has said, I believe sometimes that if in days gone by the owners of industry had been a little more considerate of their employees there might not have been feelings created against them.

Does the hon. member
think for a moment that every manufacturer has succeeded in making money? Have not many of them failed?

The tariff has nothing to
do with that question. However, if high tariffs permit the manufacturer to become prosperous, then surely the past few years have indicated that high tariffs have not been able to do anything for manufacturers in Canada.
And hundreds of thousands of working people on relief.

The hon. member for
Davenport has asked what the hon. member for York North thinks about the reductions in the duty on farm implements. I am in favour of the reductions; that is what I think of them. I tell him that, because the farmers of Canada, if they wish to get rid of their surplus products, have to compete in the markets of the world. If they are going to do that they have to be placed in a favourable position to compete with the farmers of other countries. If we are going to hold them up on the cost of their farm implements and necessities of life, we cannot expect them ito ge,t along very well in competition with other countries.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any great length, but there are one or two matters I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members. It has been said to-day that there was a great increase in the production of farm implements in Canada from 1923 to 1930. I believe there was also a great exportation of farm implements during that period, and
that exportation was going, not to the United States but largely to European countries. Some hon. gentlemen may say: Why not continue to export to European countries? The answer is that European countries have so raised their tariffs that it is impossible to-day for the Canadian manufacturer of farm implements to export to those countries. He has no foreign market to-day; his market is the home market alone.
Considerable mention has been made of the price of farm implements. I would draw attention to the fact that the system in vogue in Canada to-day in the sale of farm implements entails considerable expense. There are many manufacturers who make their goods and then turn them over to sales people throughout the dominion; those sales people pay the manufacturer for the goods, and that is the end of it so far as the manufacturer is concerned. But in the farm implement industry the manufacturer is not only manufacturer but sales agent as well. The farmer pays directly to that manufacturer. The manufacturer makes his implements, and turns them over to some agent, say in western Canada; that agent sells to the farmer, and the farmer then gives a note to the manufacturer. Not only that, but under the laws of our provinces it is necessary for farm implement manufacturers to maintain warehouses and supply parts for every implement they sell over a period of ten years. That is one reason why the farm implement manufacturer is in a different position entirely from that of the manufacturer of practically every other manufactured commodity in this country.
A great deal has been said about high tariffs, but after all, we have in this trade agreement a tariff of 12J per cent on farm implements. Some may consider that a high tariff, but personally I do not consider it so. I consider it a reasonable tariff.
Some hon. members have said that the manufacturers should give a little more consideration to the farmer. Probably it would be well if that worked all round. Probably each of us might well give a little more consideration to the rest of us. I think each one of us thinks too much of his own particular constituency rather than of the interests of the dominion as a whole. We should look at this country as one great dominion, with the interests of one part being the concern of all. In that way only can we advance.
We cannot compare tariffs to-day with tariffs in 1923 because conditions throughout the world have so changed that we are living to-day in an entirely different world so far as economic conditions are concerned. I hope we shall all view tariff questions reasonably
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

with a view to getting this country back on its feet, not only getting the farmers back on their feet, not only getting our manufacturers busy in their plants again, not only having capital return to this dominion, but putting workmen back to work and doing all we can for the good of the country as a whole.

I am in full accord with this reduction in the tariff on agricultural implements. I would say further that when you compare the price of agricultural products with that of agricultural implements, the price of agricultural implements is too high and out of all proportion to the price of farm products to-day. I think I am correct in stating that agricultural implements enter the United States free, and therefore our Canadian manufacturers have that potential market at their doors. I think that 12J per cent should be ample protection for them.
Too much.

Yes, perhaps too much. I understand from authoritative sources that our implement manufacturers sell their products to the farmers of Russia and of other countries at a lower price than they sell to the Canadian farmer, and yet in selling our farm products we have to sell in open competition on the markets of the world. For that reason I am one hundred per cent behind the government in this reduction in the tariff on farm implements.

With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word to my hon. friend from Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) who is particularly interested, as I am, in the development of the home market. There is a difference of opinion between myself and some other members of this house as to the best way to develop the home market, but I think it is very easy to demonstrate the best way, and I now proceed to do so.
In 1922 we had a home market in Canada for 120,000,000 worth of agricultural implements-I am giving figures from the bureau of statistics. In 1930 that home market rose to $38,000,000. Then we got the kind of tariff which my hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) suggests would give us stability, but unfortunately in this case stability passed out of sight almost altogether, for in 1931 the consumption of agricultural implements in Canada dropped from $38,000,000 to $12,000,000.
What year?
In 1931 the apparent consumption of agricultural implements in Canada was $12,000,000. I am taking production, plus imports, minus exports.
Give us the world consumption.

Are we dealing with the tariff of the world or the tariff of Canada? What will the Chairman say if we drift all over the world? In 1930 the consumption in Canada was $38,000,000; in 1931, $12,000,000; in 1932, $6,000,000; in 1933, 6,000,000; in 1934, $8,000,000. The darkness deepens as the tariff rises.
Now I will take the imports of agricultural implements. We have heard protests from some hon. members that lowering the tariff would lead to increased imports from the United States, and consequently to a decrease in production of Canadian agricultural implements, but I want to give the committee the facts. In 1927 our imports were S26,000,-000; in 1928, $39,000,000; in 1929, $31,000,000. Of course, hon. members who differ from me politically will throw up their hands in holy horror when I give those figures and ask: What happened to the poor Canadian workman? Well, Mr. Chairman, in the three years in which our imports were highest the employment of Canadian labour in the production of farm implements was also highest. Those were the years 1927, 1928 and 1929. In those years wages and salaries amounted to S13.000.000, $13,000,000 and $14,000,000. When the tariff was raised to the highest point ever known in Canada, wages dropped to $3,000,000, $3,000,000 and $3,000,000. These figures show that as imports rose, employment and prosperity increased and the Canadian people were happy. Does this answer the hon. member for Davenport?
No. The hon. member is forgetting all about the depression.

I am dealing with agricultural implements. I have just shown my hon. friend that in 1929 the production of agricultural implements resulted in wages of $14,000,000. My hon. friend says that he does not care what I say, but, alas, I care what he says. I am not worried about the ninety and nine sheep that are safe in the shepherd's fold; I am worried about the one that went astray. I have listened to the very interesting remarks of my hon. friend, but I think he is a splendid illustration of what might be called the last stand of unshaken valour. Hon. members will recall the words

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
used by Victor Hugo in describing the three houses which the British held as a last resort at the battle of Waterloo:
They were the last stand of unshaken valour rather than the maintenance of an important position.
My hon. friend is quite a fighter but he does not realize what is in the best interests of this country. Therefore, he cannot express what he does not know. One word as to his little book. I enjoyed that little book very much and if I had been chairman I would not have stopped his reading it.
I should like to read more.

There are some splendid things in it which I am going to use upon the public platform. It demonstrates the fact that a reciprocity agreement would be of benefit to the United States and also of benefit to Canada. It is the mutual interest of both nations that we are legislating for in this agreement. Were it not to the mutual benefit of both parties I, for one, would not want to support it because I know that by mutual benefits we go forward to prosperity, but by the attitude of my hon. friend we go backwards, as we have done since 1930.

I should like to draw attention to the fact that this particular tariff is still maintaining what I think is a particularly vicious principle, that is that Canadian [DOT] users of agricultural implements are made to pay the costs of production and overhead so that the surplus can be supplied to their competitors at a price below what Canadian users pay. To my mind that is subsidizing the competitors of the Canadian producer, and as such it is an utterly vicious principle. When the budget is brought down, I should like to see the whole thing -wiped out in connection with implements. We were told a few moments ago that if factories were to be found in some of our western cities this might change our attitude. A few moments ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) referred to such a factory in western Canada. In 1929 or 1930, certain people thought that this might happen if such a factory were erected in the city in which I happen to live. But what actually did happen? The factory was erected and while the corporation maintains the machinery and heats the building, the citizens of Canada and the citizens of that city have to maintain five or six hundred men who were brought in there to work in that factory until the factory can open up again.
Is it an agricultural implement factory to which the hon. member is referring?
I am talking about an automobile factory.
The hon. member is out of order.

I was using that to illustrate the whole system of protective tariffs. I should like to see the subsidies being paid to our foreign competitors removed entirely, and that is what I urge in relation to tariffs, and what I shall urge when this matter is considered at a later date.

A short time ago the minister complained of items being held up, but I should like to draw his attention to the fact that for the last thirty-seven minutes we have heard from practically every group but the Conservative party.

Perhaps I might be permitted to offer a suggestion to hon. members. The question of tariffs was thoroughly discussed during the recent federal elections and if ever a government received a mandate to reduce tariffs, this government did. So far as I am concerned, I am going to urge the government to reduce tariffs all along the line. In view of what the hon. member has said, I suggest that we close this discussion on tariffs and get on with the business.

I contend that we have given too much assistance to the manufacturers of farm implements. Hon. members from Toronto can make inquiries similar to those I made. I have gone through the Massey-Harris plant many times. I asked the foreman there why the plant was not running and he told me that the plant was too large for the necessities of the country. He said that the plant had been built to supply the foreign trade; that thousands of implements used to be sent out of the country, but that now the business was confined to Canada. He said that the plant was so large that it cost too much money to run it; that it did not pay to run the plant until they had thousands of machines to make. He told me that they were using sixteen tons of coal per day just to turn over the machinery in order to keep the shafts from warping.
That is what he will be doing again.

I might say to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) that when I was in his riding one of his lieutenants told me that he was one of the strongest men for reciprocity there was in the dominion.

That did not have much effect there.
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
He told me that there was no more zealous supporter of reciprocity than the hon. member.
This is not reciprocity.

I told him that I thought this was only camouflage; that we were having a manifestation of pure and simple camouflage from the hon. member who is now interrupting me. If the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) will go through the Massey-Harris plant he will find out that what I say is true.
I have gone through that plant many times.

This machinery could be built much cheaper by erecting smaller factories in the outlying towns of the provinces. It does not pay to operate a combine on fifty acres and it does not pay to operate such a large plant for the production of a small number of machines. A smaller plant which was more adapted to making the different types of machinery could get along with fewer men and the costs of the implements would be lowered. Much has been sacrified to the implement makers of Canada. We have a mandate from the people and it is high time that something was done. Before the election the Conservative party tried to make out that they were in favour of reciprocity, but that was pure camouflage.
Put them in the lethal chamber.

I do not want to hold up the items unnecessarily, but I think the minister will agree that there are at least ten items going through at the one time. The principle of protection is involved all the way through this agreement. It is an amazing spectacle to see the position in which the government finds itself with free traders to its left, free traders to its right and protectionists at its back. There is also the problem of saving industry which must be considered when the budget is brought down.

We have heard those who say that the agreement is low enough to give the farmers cheaper implements; others to his left say that the duties

should be -wiped out altogether. The hon. member for Brantford is much fairer than the others, for he suggests that both sides should be taken into consideration. He spoke very cautiously. He did not suggest that the tariff should be raised but I know he would hesitate to propose any reduction in it. It is obvious therefore that there is a great difference of opinion on the opposite side in regard to this particular item. The hon. member for Moose Jaw would no doubt say, "Hear, hear" to the removal altogether of the duties; I am sure he would approve the wiping out of the 12J per cent.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Brantford is one of the fairest-minded of the new members; he is popular in the district from -which he comes, and I know his position is entirely different. I am not pressing him for an answer, but I know he realizes that so far as the city of Brantford is concerned there is another angle from which the question is to be viewed. I rather admired the courage of the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. McNevin). I believe he would say, "Hear, hear" to the wiping out of the tariff altogether, the removing of the 12| per cent, notwithstanding what the consequence might be to the city of Lindsay.
Speak for yourself.
The hon. member for Huron-Perth himself said-
Said what?
-that he was in favour of lower tariffs all along the line.
I said that I would urge a reduction in duties all along the line and I stand by that statement.
That is what I said.
Speak for yourself.
I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman who has just interrupted would also wipe out the duties altogether.
Surely.
It is quite apparent therefore that there is a variety of opinion on the other side.
I have been called to order, Mr. Chairman. Is the hon. gentleman now in order in his catechism?

Thank you. With reference to the agricultural implement situation in Canada, there are "some features that undoubtedly stand out, and I am delighted to say that I find myself in agreement with some hon. gentlemen across the floor. I wish I could agree with the Minister of Finance, because I like him very much, more than he likes me, I think. At any rate, I agree with the hon. member for Brantford; there are two sides to the question. 1 represent people who buy farm implements; I am myself a purchaser of farm implements, and I may add that in my riding there are no manufacturers, no manufacturers in iron and steel at any rate. Having said this, let me add that I agree with the hon. member for Brantford when he says that all factors must be taken into consideration. Now I am wondering what is going to happen, who is going to benefit very much by this item. I have listened to the hon. member for York North and I presume he would favour wiping out the tariff of 12j per cent.

Why doesn't the hon.
gentleman speak for himself and tell us where he stands?

If the hon. gentleman will listen he will have no doubt where I stand on this item. I have been trying to tell the committee that I am more or less in agreement with the hon. member for Brantford, in that there are two sides to the question. We must not overlook the fact of the gradual development of Canada's industrial life, down through the years, by means of the policy of protection, including protection on farm implements. The industrial life of the country has developed through a reasonable fiscal policy, a policy of reasonable protection which has provided employment to large numbers of our citizens. That fact is admitted on the other side, because the government has maintained the tariff. Industry has endured the gibes of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition, but it has certainly enjoyed their protection, in practice, when they have been in power.
As regards the effect on the implement industry and on the home market, some of the figures kindly placed on Hansard by the Minister of Finance this afternoon reveal a gradual development since 1931. My hon. friend from Huron North has referred to a steady increase in purchases from 1922 to 1930, and that is true. We were riding on the crest of a wave of world prosperity. The increase was gradual through those years, but the increased consumption of farm implements in Canada contrasted unreasonably with the
increased percentage of consumption of foreign manufactured goods. Prior to 1930 we were importing at different times as much as we produced.
The Prime Minister lowered the tariffs between 1922 and 1930, and what happened? Some hon. gentlemen have told us that they are interested in the consumer; the hon. member for York North declares that he is interested in the purchaser of farm implements. I was buying implements in those years, and I think he will agree that the price of implements increased when his party lowered the tariff. Importations increased and the percentage of foreign production gradually came up year by year. After 1930 the tariff was increased, and I can recall members from western Canada appealing to the governments of the day, particularly to the Prime Minister, in 1931 and 1932, on the ground that the farmers, both west and east, would be called upon to pay higher prices. Well, as a purchaser of farm implements, I know that prices were and have been lower. And now we have the amazing spectacle of a member of the government asking for an investigation to find out why farm implement companies should have the privilege of raising prices when the Liberal party has the courage to reduce the tariff again.
So far as the effect on trade is concerned, this is a matter which I think should be taken seriously into consideration. The Minister of Finance has been good enough to give us the figures, and we find that since the increase in the tariffs our exports have increased, to 83,567,000 last year. Since the imperial agreements went into force our exports to the British market have doubled. In 1935 we exported 83,567,000 worth; and in 1931, before the tariffs were raised, we imported approximately $16,500,000 worth of agricultural implements and exported, I believe, less than 81,000,000.
That was in 1931 and 1932.

The result has
been, that even during the year of depression referred to, we imported the product of a foreign workshop to the tune, even at my hon. friend's figures, of approximately 89,000,000 or $10,000,000, goods that could have been made in Canada, giving employment to additional workmen. At the same time the farmers of York North as well as those of Dufferin paid more for their farm implements than they did when they were

buying them from manufacturers in the city of Brantford. If	there are	two sides tothis; if it will help manufacturers and labour men in the cities who are waiting and wondering what is going to happen; if it will help farmers by developing the home market, and if it will keep in this country millions of dollars which would otherwise go to a country to which we have to send to pay	our	debt,	a million	dollars everyday the sun rises, then I say that this question should be very gravely considered. If it would reduce prices to the farmers, I would be willing to suggest that the duty should be lowered still more. But I have had three experiences in this house; I have watched	the	price	go up when the tariffwent down; I have watched the price go down when -the tariff went up, and I have watched	the	price	again go	up when the
tariff again came down. So surely three times is out.

They stayed down from the time the then Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) raised the tariff until the time my hon. friend's party came into power, or after they came into power.

effect until this winter. Hon. members shake their heads. Can the hon. member tell me when prices went down?

I want to correct
the hon. member. With all respect to him, while prices may have been discounted in

respect of implements sold in the west, the price of farm implements in eastern Canada did not rise until very recently, about three months ago. The price list was out, I think, on February 1.

may have been withdrawn as far as western Canada is concerned, but it made no difference to the price in Ontario.

The price stayed
in force in Ontario; evidently it made no difference. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) has evidently stayed true to form. He seems to have clung fast to that old dusty doctrine of free trade, which has been thrown out of the back door by every other country in the world. This afternoon, when I listened to him, I thought it would be interesting to hear him speak for his colleague the member for Brantford (Mr. Macdonald), and see the excellent reception he would get if he made the same kind of speech in the city of Brantford.
I accept the invitation.

So far as the
principle is concerned we have had a good lesson in this country. We have watched developments when the government changed: we remember when the Minister of Finance opposed the policy of brick for brick, and said that it would absolutely ruin the agriculture of this dominion.

Mr. Chairman, citation
552 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms seems to make the general principle quite clear. It says:
Though it is the function of the committee of ways and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes . .. amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of
equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty, the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown.

Mr. Chairman, may I say just a word with regard to this motion being made at this particular time. As the committee is aware, we are considering an item in a schedule to an agreement which has been signed on the part of each of two countries. We are not in the position of the committee of ways and means considering budget items in the ordinary course. We are considering whether or not we shall accept *this agreement in its entirety or so alter it as to make its acceptance impossible. The agreement has been signed by the Secretary

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of State of the United States on behalf of the United States, and by myself on behalf of Canada. It was signed on the understanding that both in the United States and in Canada an effort would be made to have the agreement accepted in its entirety in the form in which it was signed. The President of the United States has since proclaimed the agreement and it has the full force of that proclamation in the United States at the present time. I should feel that it would be a distinct violation of the terms of the agreement itself and the basis upon which it was entered into were we at this time to seek to alter any of its particulars. We must either accept the agreement as a whole or we must realize that if we are going to alter it in any particular it may have the effect of rendering the entire agreement invalid. I am, as respects the duties on agricultural implements, rather of the same mind as the hon. member who has made this motion. I should like to see the duties on agricultural implements reduced further and perhaps at a later time in this session I shall try to use what influence I have with the Minister of Finance to see if he may not reduce them. I cannot say whether he will or not, but I think my bon. friend would be only prejudicing that for which he stands if he presses his motion at this time. If that is done, I shall have to ask the committee to reject the motion, should it not meanwhile be ruled out of order.

It will be recalled that before I made my motion I asked if it were permissible to introduce such a motion. I was told to put it in writing, after which time it would be considered. It struck me to-day that we were having an interminable discussion upon these matters and that there was a large body of opinion in this committee in favour of eliminating these particular duties. I felt it would be in the interests of the people of the dominion, at least of those whom we represent in western Canada, to see if the government would not accept a motion of this description and eliminate the duties on all farm implements. I have before me a report compiled by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) showing what the tariff costs the various parts of Canada. In 1931 the tariff cost the province, a part of which I represent, over $25,000,000. Let us bear in mind that of the total area of cultivated land in Canada amounting to 73,000,000 acres, 55,000,000 acres lie between the great lakes and the Rocky mountains. I recognize the mandate that the government has in relation to freer trade, and it seems to me that this would be an initial step which would be welcomed by the people in the farm-

I think our objective should be to induce Canadian manufacturers to make as much equipment as they can in this country and so give employment to other Canadians.

4. That it has accordingly been arranged with the German government to exchange the conventional tariff of Germany in return for the intermediate tariff of Canada for a period of nine months from April 1, 1933

For a number of years prior to 1930 we imported on the average from the United States about twenty-five million feet of lumber at an average value of $1,500,000. One would have thought, with that tremendous advantage that Canada had, this was one item which our Conservative friends would have left severely alone. But no, sir. Lumber in the finished state entering Canada bore an ad valorem duty of 25 per cent, while lumber in the rough was free. Things were going along nicely until 1931 when our Conservative friends were nicely established in office, and



Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
were looking around, I suppose, for some new place to apply their Canada First policy. In 1931 they applied to the imports of lumber from the United States an arbitrary valuation of $18 per thousand. Let me give one illustration. Hardwood flooring of a certain kind imported from the southern United States was sold there for $60 a thousand. That was the regular price charged in the United States, not a dumping price. Our Conservative friends added an arbitrary $18 to that $60, bringing the value to $78 for duty purposes. That was in the spring of 1931. But not content with that, on the first of June, 1932, encouraged by the success of these government measures, the Canadian manufacturers waited on the government and secured the imposition of an additional S18 per thousand specific duty against the importation of lumber into Canada.
What kind of lumber?

Hardwood lumber, of course. The action of the Canadian government was immediately followed by action on the part of producers of hardwood lumber in the southern states. They raised the price of their hardwood flooring to $78, the kind they had been selling for $60. So what actually happened was that the action by the Conservative government at Ottawa transferred $18 per thousand from the pockets of Canadian consumers into those of American producers. Again the Canadian consumers paid the price.

Does the hon.
member state that the Canadian government put on an extra duty of $18?
Yes; that is what I am saying.
Eighteen dollars per thousand.
I got this information from the department. This is what happened under the regime of my hon. friends.
They cannot believe what they did.
A little later, in 1932, our hon. friends opposite, encouraged by the success they had so far, added a one per cent excise duty to all imports of lumber coming into Canada.
That was not only on lumber; it was on everything.

Yes; but I am dealing with
lumber just now. We are on the lumber item.

Why try to create the impression that it was on lumber alone.
IMr. Ward.]

It is the privilege of my hon. friend to introduce this question at any other time. Let us see what was the effect of this upon the employment of Canadian lumber men. In 1930 there were 3,000 sawmills in operation in Canada, all interested directly or indirectly in lumber exports, and less than one dozen of these plants interested in imports of hardwood. In the interests of that one dozen small, picayune and insignificant plants employing a few dozen workmen, our hon. friends opposite destroyed to a large extent an export trade of one billion feet. By and large our export trade exceeded our import trade by about forty to one. We did export, prior to 1931, forty thousand feet to every thousand feet we imported.
That is good business.
Yes; but you destroyed it.
Why kill it?
What was the effect upon the American government when our hon. friends opposite imposed the one per cent excise duty and the extra $18 per thousand feet specific duty?
My hon. friend must be reading his notes incorrectly. There has never been an $18 per thousand feet specific duty on lumber since confederation.
I stand by what I have stated. I received these figures from the department.
Then the hon. gentleman must be misinterpreting them or misconstruing their effect.
I think the hon. member is sticking very closely to his text.
He is sticking closer to that than he is to the facts.

I can understand why my hon. friends are getting uneasy. I intend to point out in a few moments that this one act on the part of the Conservative government put out of work something like 28,000 men who were engaged in the lumbering industry. That is the number estimated by the Lumbermen's News, of about eight or nine months ago. When my hon. friend for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) gets up and talks about employment being given to some workmen in a little industry in Toronto, or the effect that this agreement will have upon the employment of a few men, I want to point out that it would hardly be possible for

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
anything contained in this agreement to have the same effect upon employment in this country as have some of the acts of my hon. friends opposite. I can quite understand why they are anxious to cover up their tracks.
I am not going to take back anything I said.

In 1932 the American government, I think I am correct in saying in retaliation for the action of our hon. friends opposite, made another change in their rates of duties. The tariff arrangements of the United States they obtained in 1930 had existed since 1911. The American government at this time, owing to the action of the Canadian government, imposed a duty of S4 per thousand feet against the importation of all Canadian lumber. This was to replace the $1 per thousand feet previously imposed on our dressed lumber.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that there was no duty before 1930?
I did not say that at all.

What was the
duty on lumber going into the United States under the Hawley-Smoot tariff?

The tariff arrangement as of 1930 had existed from 1911 up to that time. The duty was SI per thousand feet on finished lumber, while lumber dressed on one side and in the rough entered the United States free of duty.

What kind of
lumber was the SIS per thousand feet specific duty imposed upon?

I have just given that. That
was the specific duty applied on finished hardwood lumber coming into Canada. An arbitrary value for duty purposes was placed on lumber finished on one side. Let us see the effect this had upon the lumbering industry. According to the Lumbermen's News, on December 1, 1935, of the 3,000 mills which had been in operation in 1930 only seventy-five of the larger mills were operating. By 1935 two of the largest spruce mills in Canada were in the hands of the receiver, due to the tariff meddling by the government of our hon. friends opposite. One mill with headquarters at Edmonton and manufacturing 225 million feet a year went into the hands of the receiver because of this impost of $4 per thousand feet which had been placed against softwood entering the United States. This action had been taken by the American government in retalia-12739-741
tion for the actions of the former government.

Does my hon. friend
know that that was in retaliation for some action on our part or in pursuance of some domestic policy being carried out in connection with their housing program?

I have obtained most of my
information from the Lumbermen's News. This publication is not put out by the Liberals or Progressives; it is published and supported by the lumbermen of Canada who are interested in the success of their business. Since 1930 I have been reading Hansard very studiously, but I have not seen one reference by the hon. member for Davenport to his own government having put men out of employment. I think we have had just enough of the kind of stuff we have been getting from the other side of this house. I was informed the other day by the officials of a certain department that right now duties ranging from 100 to 200 per cent are being imposed against articles coming into Canada. Yet we have hon. friends opposite rising to their feet and protesting against these duties. The thing is all on one side. They have been protesting continually against the lowering of duties on any little item, with no thought whatsoever of the effect it may have on the farmers of this Country. I wonder where the revenue came from to build all	the palatial homes	to be found	inthe	city	of Toronto,	from	which my hon.
friend from Davenport comes.
Good Canadian workmen built them and the stuff that went into them.

In every case the people from the countryside had to pay through the nose for protection given the manufacturers, without	any	compensating	factor.	I am here	inthe	interests of freer	trade;	I was sent	to
demand freer trade for the benefit of the consumers of Canada. I agree with my hon. friend from Brantford who spoke this afternoon, and if we follow his philosophy we shall not have 'any tariffs at all in Canada.
Not Brantford.

Tariffs are always imposed in the interests of a small percentage of the people. If we considered the interests of the people as a whole we would not have tariffs at all. The trouble with our friends from the industrial centres is that they see only their own small world. Perhaps if I were in the position of my hon. friend from Davenport I would do as he does; but if he would visit some of the homes in the country and see the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
conditions under which the farmers operate, where piles of junk are masquerading as farm machinery and where there are many other conditions comparable with that, he would be a little more considerate when he asks for high protection for industries that are at present over-protected, with large profits a fair share of which they do not pass on to the labouring population. If he studied the price spreads report he would be impressed by the extent to which that condition has prevailed.
Order.

I realize that I am a little beside the point and I wonder that you did not call me to order, Mr. Chairman. I want to thank the Prime Minister for having secured for Canadian lumber freer entry into the United States, which will result in putting back to work between 20,000 and 30,000 men in the next few years.

I do not know where the hon. member for Dauphin got his information; if he will read over the report in Hansard to-morrow and make further inquiries he will find that he is in error in many respects. He thanks the Prime Minister for the free admission of lumber into the United States, but that is not in keeping with the facts. With regard to the duty on lumber going into the United States, this has been a difficult question in Canada throughout the years, during the whole of my lifetime. It has been under discussion many times and jhis extra charge put on lumber in 1932 by the United States was not in any sense in retaliation because of anything we had done; it was imposed at the special request of the lumbermen of the United States, particularly of the western states. I believe that if we had time to look into the question it would be found that they went to Washington on a special mission for the purpose of getting this extra impost put on. There has never been a time in my memory when Canada was not ready and willing to have reciprocity with the United States, to have reciprocal arrangements with them in connection with lumber. The offer has been made them several times, and the hon. gentleman is entirely in error in thinking that their duty was put on because of anything we had done. There was a time when we could send our lumber into the United States without a duty but that was for a short period. Nearly all through the years the United States insisted on collecting a duty on lumber from Canada, and the rate has varied from time to time. Practically, however, there has always been a duty on our lumber going into the United States.
If what the hon. gentleman says is correct, it is strange that the Prime Minister was able to secure so promptly freer entry of rough lumber into the United States.

I know a little about lumber and I know what the effect of this agreement will be in British Columbia. I will not take up the time of the committee going into the history of this matter, but in 1931 when the duty of $4 a thousand was imposed by the United Slates government, dozens of sawmills in British Columbia's interior, along the lines of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, closed their doors, throwing hundreds of men on relief. This fall, when the news came out that they had taken off almost $2, all these sawmills put men into the bush again to cut logs, taking back hundreds of men. They went further. The logging association of British Columbia increased the wages of those men they took back from $7.50 to $15 a month, without being asked by the union to do so. What I have said in regard to the fisheries will apply to lumbering in British Columbia. This agreement will be a life saver so far as British Columbia is concerned. Thousands of men will be put back to work at better wages than they have been receiving, and mills that have been closed for five years are now working. Spruce is not affected by quota, and we shall have the benefit of the reduction from 84 to $2 per thousand, which will mean to the lumbermen from $40 to $60 a carload. The government, in my opinion, has taken a step in the right direction and I hope that some day we shall have free access to the United States for our Canadian lumber.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What about arbitrary
valuations?

It might be termed an arbitrary valuation on valuations for duty purposes or placed against them, it is true, as the hon. member says, at $18 a thousand, but a valuation of SIS and a tariff against lumber coming in at $18 are two entirely different matters. That is, so far as our importations are concerned they are entirely different. The hon. member mentioned that we do not import one thousand feet where we had formerly imported forty thousand, and it is intimated that this $4 a thousand has destroyed the lumber industry in Canada. To some extent it affected it, but I know that as regards the industry throughout the country it will also be agreed that, due to the imperial trade agreement, due to the increased tariff, due to the fixed value for duty purposes if you will, the number of those employed in the lumber industry in general in Canada from coast to coast increased almost three times since 1931, before the agreements. There were just three times as many employed in 1935 in the lumber industry in this country as there were just prior to the imperial trade agreement, due to the fact that that agreement made it possible for the industry to export just six times as much lumber as was formerly exported. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) will agree, I know, that it increased substantially the prosperity of the lumber industry in British Columbia.
He voted against it.

I do not want to hold up the committee, but I think it is unfair to say that the increase of tariffs by the former government in any way decreased the employment of lumbermen, when in 1931 and the beginning of 1932 we had every yard from coast to coast filled with unsold lumber. I repeat again that, due to the policies of the government he has recently been condemning, the government which was in power from 1930 to 1935, even in a time of depression, when world trade was shrinking to one-third of its former volume, those employed in the industry increased from
45,000	to 120,000. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) laughs, but I say that it is just similar to the position his rayon company at Sherbrooke would be in if tariffs had been lowered further, and this commodity had been allowed to come into Canada instead of arrangements being made for sales outside of this country. Then we would have had a different tale.
We are talking about lumber.
Isn't it lumber we are speaking about?
You are speaking of stockings.
Again I repeat that the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) was unfair to himself, I think.
With reference to the last speaker attributing the increased price ol lumber to the Ottawa agreements-
Increased sales.

Increased sales or price, he is entirely wrong as far as Ontario is concerned. The fact that the Ontario government reduced stumpage dues from $4 to $2 a thousand1 gave an impetus to the manufacture and sale of lumber far beyond anything the last government did in that connection.

I have listened to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe as he spoke very highly of the attainments of the late government with regard to the export of lumber. I live in a lumber district, and the yards were not full of lumber when the preceding Liberal government was in power, but as soon as his government came into power in 1931 exports of lumber to the United States stopped completely. The yards were full of lumber that could not be sold and the lumberjacks were out of work. That is not all. Our best exports before that went to our neighbouring country, the United States. The leader of the former government thought it wise to divert our trade to the United Kingdom, and he messed the job completely; it was an utter failure. The Tory party is responsible for the decrease in the lumber trade. Whatever they say they cannot change the facts; they are guilty of that great offence of destroying the lumber trade of this country. That is the fact, and every lumber man is a witness to it.

I should like to ask as
a matter of information: Is it not necessary for a member to speak from his own chair?

Not in committee.
Sir GEORGE PERI.EY: Will the minister be good enough to tell us for the benefit of all members of this house, what the rate into the United States of ordinary Canadian sawn lumber is under this agreement?
